10974-a-ride-to-india-across-persia-and-:
Harry de Windt rode overland to India in the 1890s and published this illustrated account in 1891. Starting at Tiflis and Baku, he crossed the Caspian to Persia, travelled through Resht, Teheran, Isfahan, and Shiraz, then pushed through Baluchistan to Kelat, Quetta, and Bombay. Herbert Walker's illustrations, drawn from the author's sketches, picture desert sunrises, caravanserais, and nomad camps.

De Windt writes as a seasoned traveller, frank about disappointments such as Persepolis, which he found less picturesque than Rome or Pompeii, and warm about Shiraz in moonlight. He notes British tourists carving names into ruins with shame. The book gives a lively route through lands few Europeans then crossed on horseback, with practical detail and sharp personal judgment.
13333-correspondence-conversations-of-al:
Correspondence and Conversations of Alexis de Tocqueville with Nassau William Senior, volume two, London 1872, covers 1834 to 1859, edited by M. C. M. Simpson. Its journal for 1851 to 1852 tracks the army as master of France, the coup planned for March 1852, socialism leading to despotism, and Louis Napoleon's devotion to the Pope. The volume is a primary record of French politics.

One passage paints a statesman in blinkers, seeing only the English Constitution straight ahead, blind to France on either side, yet leading the centre gauche into most of its errors. Another notes Tocqueville's claim that a man can be original only in his own tongue, since in others he says only what he can recall. The book is essential for students of Tocqueville and the Second Empire.
13990-the-fugitive-slave-law-and-its-vic:
The American Anti-Slavery Society published this 1856 tract, number eighteen, on the Fugitive Slave Law and its victims. Congress enacted the law in September 1850, signed by Speaker Howell Cobb and Senate president William R. King, and approved by Millard Fillmore on September 18. Authorship is generally ascribed to James M. Mason of Virginia.

The tract lists votes, including Northern representatives who backed the bill, and Southern opponents. It then tells stories of captured fugitives and their families. The authors aim to stir public anger against the law. The tract suits readers of abolitionist literature. It documents how a statute became a moral crisis.
17466-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
Scribner and Company issued this October 1878 number of St. Nicholas, volume five, number twelve, a magazine made for boys and girls. The issue opens with Edith Hawkins's story The Violin Village. It is set in Mittenwald on the borders of the Tyrol, a village shut in by high mountains where simple, hard-working folk chiefly make stringed musical instruments. Fine days show the instruments drying outdoors.

As a single monthly number, the issue mixes stories, pictures, and pieces meant to amuse and instruct young readers of the 1870s. Its pages capture the tone of a leading American children's magazine, earnest, cheerful, and fond of far places. Readers today get a snapshot of what children were offered for reading matter in the autumn of 1878.
19399-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
A January issue of St. Nicholas magazine for boys and girls dates from January of eighteen seventy-eight. It opens with a medieval tale, The Ravens and the Angels, set round a cathedral that served as a father's house for rich and poor alike. Fairy play, a modern William Tell game, and pictures of mail carriers follow.

The mix is typical of the magazine at its best: stories, games, and facts side by side, all aimed at young minds. It shows how the leading children's magazine of the age taught wonder, humor, and good conduct in one sitting.
19594-the-eugenic-marriage-volume-1-of-4:
W. Grant Hague, a New York physician, wrote this first volume of a four-volume guide to the eugenic marriage, published in the mid nineteen teens. It presents itself as a personal guide to better living and better babies, with an index covering all four volumes.

Passages praise mothers' milk over artificial food, even from poorly fed mothers, and urge mothers to preach and practice nursing. The book is a period document of the eugenics movement, now discredited, and it should be read as history, not as medical advice. The opening chapter ties the science to infant mortality, heredity, environment, and education in turn.
21418-the-eugenic-marriage-volume-4-of-4:
Volume four of W. Grant Hague's The Eugenic Marriage, issued in 1913, closes his guide to better living and better babies. Hague was a New York doctor trained at Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons. He wrote in the name of eugenics, then a much-praised new science.

The pages give rules for the care of young children in the home. Hague warns against letting babies crawl on cold floors, where draughts run low. Beds, sofas, or raised boards are urged for play instead. Modern readers will read the book as a record of its age, since eugenics is now rejected and condemned.
24854-the-eugenic-marriage-volume-2-of-4:
W. Grant Hague, a New York doctor, published this second volume of The Eugenic Marriage in 1914, subtitled a personal guide to better living and better babies. The volume centers on sex hygiene for boys, under the heading Building Our Boys, and it opens with a Better Babies contest winner held up as a model child.

Hague writes for parents, warning of venereal disease in town and country alike and urging frank, early teaching. The book speaks in the earnest, moral voice of the eugenics movement of its day. It now reads as a frank record of how doctors of 1914 linked health, morals, and the future of the race.
25044-the-eugenic-marriage-volume-3-of-4:
Volume three of W. Grant Hague's Eugenic Marriage, a four-volume personal guide published in New York in 1916, carries the early twentieth-century doctrine of eugenics into advice on married life. Hague, a New York physician, frames marriage as a formative period in which temperament, habits, and health shape the home children grow up in.

Chapters take up the best age to marry, clashes of temper, the wedding night, the honeymoon, the first months of wifehood, and the slow work of two people adjusting to one another. Modern readers will find its science dated and its claims about better babies tied to ideas now discredited, but the volume documents how widely eugenic thinking reached into ordinary domestic advice.
26893-the-new-avatar-and-the-destiny-of-:
Jirah D. Buck, author of Mystic Masonry and A Study of Man, published this work in a second edition at Chicago in 1916, copyrighted 1911. Its subtitle promises the findings of natural science reduced to practical studies in psychology. Its sixteen chapters divide into two sections: studies in psychology, then the new avatar of natural science. Buck dedicates the book to great friends, helpers visible and invisible, whose aim is to encourage, uplift, and inspire.

Early chapters classify faculties, capacities, and powers, weigh empirical and scientific evidence, and treat mediumship, seership, and hypnosis. Later chapters trace indebtedness to ancient India, hero worship and folklore, portents of the present time, and the separable soul in folklore. Buck's stated principles run through all: the animal principle is selfishness, the divine one altruism, and truth is tested by its use and beneficence.
27740-a-letter-to-the-right-honorable-th:
John Haslam, a London physician with nearly thirty years of work on insanity, addressed this 1823 letter to the Lord Chancellor on unsoundness of mind and imbecility of intellect. He wrote as an experienced medical man whose patients' cases often came before the courts.

Haslam argues that doctors disagreed sharply about the nature of mental derangement, and that the law needed clearer medical guidance when judging whether a person could manage their affairs. The letter is an early plea for closer ties between medicine and the courts in questions of sanity.
27848-hymns-of-the-greek-church-translat:
John Brownlie translated these Hymns of the Greek Church with introduction and notes, published in Edinburgh and London by Oliphant, Anderson and Ferrier in 1900. The volume brings some sixty simple and powerful hymns into dignified church English.

Press notices praised Brownlie's taste and poetic gift, noting that his verses rarely betray the translator's hand. The book introduced English readers to the richness of the Greek liturgy and to the religious thought of the early and medieval Eastern church. Brownlie notes that this cheap form follows the first series by ten years, after a decade of hymnal revision.
2836-abraham-lincoln-and-the-union-a-chr:
Nathaniel Stephenson wrote this short history of Abraham Lincoln and the Union for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918. The volume covers the Civil War years from Lincoln's side, following the president, his cabinet, and the northern public through secession, compromise efforts, and war. Stephenson warns that no brief book can settle every dispute about the era.

The narrative stresses the political work of holding the North together, including figures such as Crittenden and Everett and the search for a settlement that might save the Union. Lincoln stands at the center as a manager of competing pressures rather than a distant hero. The book suits readers who want a compact, readable account of the embattled North.
28384-as-i-remember-recollections-of-ame:
Marian Gouverneur wrote As I Remember in 1911 as recollections of American society during the nineteenth century. Gouverneur, dedicating the book to her father, Judge James Campbell, and her husband, Samuel L. Gouverneur Jr., recalls early Long Island days, New Yorkers, schooldays, and life in the metropolis. D. Appleton and Company published the illustrated volume.

Later chapters cover Long Branch, Newport, fashion and letters, Washington in the forties, social leaders, and the diplomatic corps. Gouverneur writes with warmth and gossip, naming distinguished acquaintances. The book offers a rich, personal view of old New York and Washington society.
30406-benjamin-franklin-a-picture-of-the:
John S. C. Abbott presents Benjamin Franklin as a picture of the struggles of the infant American nation one hundred years earlier, copyrighted in 1876. Next to George Washington, Abbott writes, Franklin stands first among American patriots on the catalogue of names.

Abbott claims many virtues for Franklin and few imperfections, and promises a perfectly accurate view of his character. He follows Franklin through the great struggle that secured American independence, aiming for a vivid picture within a short compass. The book belongs to the American Pioneers and Patriots series, written for young and general readers.
30924-thirty-seven-days-of-peril-from-sc:
T. C. Everts wrote this first-person account of thirty-seven days of peril, printed in Scribner's Monthly, volume 3, number 1, in November 1871. Everts, commissioned Assessor of Internal Revenue for Montana in 1861, writes about his wanderings on an expedition to the Upper Yellowstone. He had read the magazine's May and June descriptions of the region's wonders with satisfaction, having himself shared its pleasures and suffered all its perils.

A desire to visit a remarkable region, of which he had heard marvelous accounts during several years' residence in Montana, led him to join the expedition of August last. The stupendous scenery of the Rocky Mountains had prepared his mind to credit all the wild strange stories told of the Yellowstone. He felt as certain of its physical wonders on the morning the company started from Helena as when he afterwards beheld them. It is a vivid early account of Yellowstone exploration.
38590-the-story-of-anna-kingsford-and-ed:
The Story of Anna Kingsford and Edward Maitland is a faith book by Edward Maitland, shaped past his death by Samuel Hopgood Hart. This is its third and grown form, out in nineteen five. Its full name adds the new word of the true sense of the old books. Two lines head it, that the days of plain show pass and the word of true sense comes.

Parts treat the call of the pair, their first lives, and their sense of a set task. A next part tells of a wash of the soul and of a voice that found at last a man past whom it could speak. The shared work, a dream train with no hand on its wheel, and scenes of the old books won back take heads. A seer wife and her tie to an old god fill the rows.
42810-subspeciation-in-the-kangaroo-rat-:
Subspeciation in the Kangaroo Rat, Dipodomys ordii, by Henry Setzer, is a monograph of the University of Kansas. It forms number twenty three of the first volume of the Museum of Natural History publications. The paper runs from page 473 to page 573 of that volume. Twenty seven figures and seven tables go with the text.

The issue is dated December 27, 1949, at Lawrence, Kansas. An introduction and a chapter on methods open the study proper. Paleontology and the phylogeny of the species follow in the contents. Setzer measures skins and skulls to sort the races of the rat. Kangaroo rats hop the deserts of the west on great hind feet. His monograph maps how one species splits into local forms across that range.
43391-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons Popular Science Monthly for the last month of the age past is one sheet of a famed science press for plain folk. A son of its first hand now ran the sheet. This bound part holds a half year of its sheets, from the fall to the spring.

Its rights were held by its house as the new year came in. Its parts for this month open with the wheat growth strength of the free states. Then comes a study of the lands and stocks of Europe, on the Jews, by a chair of a great school, with prints. School play grounds for the farms and small towns take third place. The sheet was the great pipe of new lore to the homes of its day.
43695-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons' Popular Science Monthly for February 1899 makes up part of volume fifty-four, edited by William Jay Youmans. The magazine was established by his father, Edward Youmans. Contents open with Stephen Smith on vegetation as a remedy for the summer heat of cities.

Other articles review Mivart's groundwork of science, praise the science of observation, and describe Death Gulch as a natural bear-trap, with illustrations. The labour problem in the tropics, principles of taxation, and a great bombardment follow. A short history of scientific instruction and the earliest writing in France round the number out. Readers get American popular science at the century's turn, miscellany and all.
44435-the-centenary-garland-being-pictor:
The Centenary Garland offers pictorial illustrations of the novels of Sir Walter Scott. Nimmo published it at Edinburgh in 1871, a hundred years after Scott birth. George Cruikshank and other artists of eminence drew the plates for the garland. Descriptions and a memoir of Scott go with the pictures in the book.

A verse by Captain Charles Gray opens the front matter in praise of Scott. Who comes alone with soul of fire and in his hand the Border lyre, it asks. He sweeps the strings and old times live again in the strain of that poem. It is Scott, great master of his art, the verse answers its own question. The novels are pictured in their order of publication through the volume.
44725-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons' Popular Science Monthly was edited by William Jay Youmans at New York, and this file holds the November 1899 number, first of a bound half year that ran to April 1900. The monthly carried science and public questions to general readers. Its lead essay, by Franklin Smith, takes up the real problems of democracy.

Smith laughs at the schemes of reformers who would save democracy by devices against fraud, corporations, and drink. Their problems, he argues, are the problems of despotism, which every tyrant has worked at to his subjects' ruin. Democracy, for him, is a condition of freedom under moral control, where a man may do as he likes so long as he leaves others the same right. The essay sets the tone of a lively, argumentative number.
45443-jack-the-young-explorer-a-boy-s-ex:
George Bird Grinnell wrote this boy's adventure, printed by Frederick A Stokes of New York with a 1908 copyright, in its eighth printing by September of that year. Jack's other tales line the front: Jack the Young Cowboy, Jack the Young Trapper, and Jack Among the Indians. Grinnell also wrote Pawnee Hero Stories and Blackfoot Lodge Tales. A plate shows a tent shaking with groans and growls from inside.

Jack rides the train into Helena, scanning the platform for his friend Hugh. Chapters take him through historic land and the Blackfoot Agency, into the unknown Northwest of the title. Grinnell, a famed hand on Indians and game, writes the frontier as he knew it, for boys who dreamed of it.
47397-zion-national-park-bryce-canyon-ce:
Zion National Park, Bryce Canyon, Cedar Breaks, Kaibab Forest, and the North Rim of Grand Canyon fill a Union Pacific System guide issued at Omaha in 1925. It was put out under the name of Murray, the road's general passenger agent. The book calls the country the land of flaming canyons and jeweled amphitheatres. South of the thirty-eighth parallel, Utah steps down in great terraces from the Wasatch summits to the Rio Virgen.

The guide reads the land in three parts: the High Plateaus, the Terraced Plateaus, and the Grand Canyon Platform. More than a hundred miles stretch from Cedar Breaks to Bright Angel Point on the canyon's rim. Ranch villages of adobe, cliff dwellings, and wild mustangs fill out the scene. Railroads sold the parks with books like this one, mixing geology, scenery, and invitation in equal parts.
49326-the-osage-tribe-two-versions-of-th:
Francis La Flesche records a ceremony in The Osage Tribe: Two Versions of the Child-Naming Rite, from the Forty-third Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, printed at Washington in 1928. The report covers the years 1925 and 1926, and this study runs from page 23 to page 164 of it. Ritual speeches, called wi-gi-e, fill most of the text.

Two gentes give their versions: the Puma gens and the Tsi-zhu Wa-shta-ge gens, each with birth names for the first three sons and daughters. The child is passed from gens to gens to be blessed, and the gentile hair cut follows.
49718-the-desultory-man-collection-of-an:
The Desultory Man came out at Paris in 1836, in a large set of British novels and romances. The title page names no author, but notes past works called Richelieu and The Gypsy. A long dedication to Miss M L Boyle tells how the work was made, and why it now seeks the public.

The writer says most of the papers were made years back for a small circle of friends. Some were printed with no name in journals, and won praise there. Friends warned of harsh reviews and of hopes dashed, yet the writer held on. Readers get a tale framed by a candid tale of its own birth, and of a young writer urged to try the same path.
49890-the-mentor-american-landscape-pain:
The Mentor, a guide magazine that called itself a wise and faithful friend, gave its twenty-sixth number to American landscape painters. Samuel Isham wrote the text. Six names head the issue: Inness, Martin, Wyant, Moran, Tryon, and Church.

Isham starts with the bare beginnings of art in America. At first, he says, all was portrait work, by rough hands from the mother country. Copley, Stuart, and Sully raised that school to worth by 1800. Landscape came late: no man gave himself to it whole till Thomas Doughty in 1820. Doughty quit the leather trade at twenty-seven to paint the land, and a school was born.
51778-the-illustration-of-books-a-manual:
Joseph Pennell teaches how drawings are made and copied for books in talks given at the Slade School, University College. The Century Co in New York and T Fisher Unwin in London issued the manual for students. Pennell had written on pen drawing and on modern picture work before these talks.

Eleven talks move from what illustration is to the tools of the trade and line work for the press. Wash drawings, wood engraving, lithography, and etching each get a full talk of their own. Later talks cover the printing of etchings and photo-based methods such as photogravure. Pennell states in his preface that the talks were among the first in the land to set out all methods side by side. Some talks first ran in the Art Journal.
53033-the-turquoise-story-book-stories-a:
The Turquoise Story Book, stories and legends of summer and nature, was compiled by Ada and Eleanor Skinner and published by Duffield of New York in 1918. It belongs to the Jewel Series, whose volumes stand listed at the front at a dollar seventy-five net each: Diamond, Emerald, Ruby, Sapphire, and Topaz beside it. A frontispiece in colour by Maxfield Parrish, Summer, opens the book.

The contents are a summer anthology. Eleanor Skinner's Iroquois legend, How Summer Conquered Winter, stands near the front, with an Australian legend of the flowers and a Japanese legend of the sun-goddess. The Summer Maker, an Ojibway legend retold from Schoolcraft, follows Lowell's June. Pieces by Burroughs, Thomas, and Trowbridge appear by special arrangement with their publishers. The Skinners had edited the Emerald and Topaz books before, and merry tales and nursery tales from many lands besides.
53559-the-courtships-of-queen-elizabeth-:
The Courtships of Queen Elizabeth is a history by Martin Hume, issued in 1896. Its subtitle names its theme: the talks for her marriage. Hume edited the Spanish state papers of her reign. That work put the day-by-day record in his hands. The book runs to sixteen chapters and an index. A portrait of the queen from Hampton Court fronts it.

In the preface Hume faults the broad-brush historians. They call the queen fickle, he says, without cause. The papers show a fixed purpose under shifting talk. Suitor after suitor came from the courts of Europe. Each bid served a plan of state as much as of love. Hume reads the bids in strict time order. His aim is a fair view of her policy. The book made her marriage game a study in statecraft.
53967-memoirs-of-the-life-exile-and-conv:
Count de Las Cases set down the life, exile, and conversations of the Emperor Napoleon from talks at St Helena. Henry Colburn issued a new edition at London in 1836, as volume one of four. Portraits and many plates support the text.

A front plate shows Napoleon on board the Bellerophon, and views of Longwood, his exile home, appear inside. Portraits of his father Charles and his mother Letizia face early pages. Las Cases presents the fallen emperor in his own words, day by day. Court, war, and island exile mix in the record. Later volumes add Josephine, Talleyrand, and Sir Hudson Lowe to the cast.
53968-memoirs-of-the-life-exile-and-conv:
Memoirs of the Life, Exile, and Conversations of the Emperor Napoleon, volume two, is by the Count de Las Cases. Colburn published this new edition in London in 1836. Portraits and numerous other embellishments accompany the text. A portrait of Josephine published in 1836 fronts this volume. Bentley printed it in London, with sellers in Edinburgh and Dublin. The whole work runs to four volumes in this edition. Las Cases shared Napoleon's exile on Saint Helena. He recorded the fallen emperor's talk day by day there.

His journal became the gospel of the Napoleonic legend in Europe. The conversations range over campaigns, politics, and private life. Volume two continues that record of exile talk. English readers took the work in Bentley's stereotype pages. It shaped how the century pictured Napoleon in captivity.
53969-memoirs-of-the-life-exile-and-conv:
Memoirs of the Life, Exile, and Conversations of the Emperor Napoleon, volume three of four, was written by the Count de Las Cases. A new edition with portraits was printed at London in 1836. Las Cases had shared Napoleon's exile on Saint Helena and kept a journal of his talk. The entry for 15 July 1816 opens this stretch of the record.

About ten o'clock the Emperor entered the writer's apartment unawares, wishing to take a walk. They went toward the wood together. The headings of the day join the bill respecting their exile with Beaumarchais and the works of Cherbourg. Napoleon had found old newspapers with anecdotes of Beaumarchais. During his Consulate, the memoir notes, he had uniformly discountenanced the playwright, despite all his wit, for his bad character and gross immorality. The volume gives the exile's table talk as his companion heard it day by day.
53970-memoirs-of-the-life-exile-and-conv:
Volume Four of the Memoirs of the Life, Exile, and Conversations of the Emperor Napoleon is the last of four volumes by the Count de Las Cases. This new edition was published at London for Henry Colburn in 1836. It carries portraits and many other illustrations. Las Cases was one of the small company who followed Napoleon into exile at St Helena.

The book is kept as a journal of the exile. An entry of the 18th of October 1816 opens this portion. Napoleon had been ill all morning, dictating to the Grand Marshal. He summoned the persons of his suite one by one. Low in spirits, he tried to amuse himself with chess, then dominos, then chess again. At length he had to go back to his chamber, unable to sit up.
55317-the-meditations-of-the-emperor-mar:
The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus is a new rendering by George W Chrystal, based on the Foulis translation of 1742. Otto Schulze printed it at Edinburgh in 1902. Chrystal was a scholar of Balliol College, Oxford.

Book one opens with what Marcus learned from his kin and teachers. From his grandfather Verus he learned good manners and a check on anger. From his father memory he took a pattern of modesty and manliness. From his mother he learned piety, generosity, and a simple life far from the ways of the rich. His tutor taught him to favor no side at the races or the games, and to bear labor with few needs. Readers get the Roman emperor private notebook in clear English.
55952-memoirs-of-the-late-war-vol-1-of-2:
Volume one of war memoirs from the wars with France came out in London in 1831. An advert for a service journal fronts the volume. The book itself holds three tales by three men. Each man served and wrote what he saw with his own eyes.

Captain Cooke of the 43rd Regiment tells his own story first. He writes of militia life, fear of a French landing, Bristol quarters, and a fatal fight. The Earl of Munster gives the history of the campaign of 1809 in Portugal. Lieutenant Moodie tells of the campaign of 1814 in Holland. Marches, camps, and fights fill a plain soldier record of hard years.
55953-memoirs-of-the-late-war-vol-2-of-2:
Memoirs of the Late War, volume two of two, closes a personal narrative of the wars with France. The hosted text opens with the title page of the second volume. Bound with it is a long notice for a service journal. That journal served officers of the army and navy. The memoir form was a common way for officers to record campaigns. Such books preserved names, marches, and fights that official reports passed over.

A closing volume of this kind usually carries the war to its end. It holds the last campaigns and the author's return home. Readers of the day prized these tales for their plain detail. They showed what service felt like at ground level. The set stands as a record of British arms in that war. Volume two brings the personal story to its close.
5641-man-or-matter-introduction-to-a-spi:
Ernst Lehrs wrote Man or Matter as an introduction to a spiritual understanding of nature, based on Goethe's method of training observation and thought. The book opens with the author's search for a way to extend scientific understanding, and a meeting with Rudolf Steiner and the work arising from his teachings. Later chapters diagnose modern science's self-restriction to one-eyed, colorblind observation.

Lehrs argues that such observation leaves no true conception of force, and treats thought as both sole reality and pure non-entity for the modern spectator. Goetheanism, dynamics, levity, and counter-space follow. Readers get a thoughtful, demanding work of Goethean science, for readers open to spirit in nature.
5712-sculpture-of-the-exposition-palaces:
Juliet James describes the sculpture of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco, palace by palace and court by court. Dedicated to A Stirling Calder, who managed the execution of the sculpture, the notes honor the vast body of sculptors and their workers whose figures crowned the fair. James treats statues, groups, and fountains as a single planned decoration, not as isolated ornaments.

Readers gain a guided walk through a vanished fairground, learning what each figure meant and how it fit its building. The book suits lovers of public art, World's Fair history, and early twentieth-century American sculpture. It preserves in words a display meant to last only a season, and it helps modern readers picture the exposition's grandeur.
57205-the-little-black-princess-a-true-t:
Jeannie Gunn wrote The Little Black Princess, billed as a true tale of life in the Never-Never, the remote bush of Australia's north. Her subject is Bett-Bett, an Aboriginal child of the station country, and the chapters take their titles from her world as Gunn heard it.

The contents list a walkabout, a coronation playabout, and dances with names the typesetter wrestled into print. Chapters turn on shimy shirts, a king alright, and the search for lily root. The pictures show the homestead, dilly-bags used by women in the bush, fire sticks, and a girl's favourite quart pot. Other plates give spears and boomerangs, coolamuns, and sea-going crocodiles described as cheeky fellows. Gunn writes of the people of the station as she lived among them. Readers get an early white woman's record of bush life, told through one child.
58380-a-short-list-of-scientific-books-p:
Short List of Scientific Books is a publisher's catalogue from London. Spon Limited of 57 Haymarket issued it in September 1909 for buyers. The firm sold its own list and acted as English agent for others. Myron Clark of New York and Spon and Chamberlain stand named there. Subject heads run from agriculture and architecture to artillery in order.

Bridges and roofs, building, cement and concrete, and civil engineering follow. Dictionaries, domestic economy, drawing, and electrical work fill the middle pages. Gas engines, hydraulics, chemistry, irrigation, and logarithm tables ensue in print. Marine and mechanical engineering, mining, and town works close the list. Engineers and builders of 1909 ordered their handbooks from these pages.
59200-mr-and-mrs-se-n:
Mr and Mrs Sên is a novel by Louise Jordan Miln, printed at New York by Burt. The copyright is 1923. Miln also wrote Mr Wu, The Feast of Lanterns and The Green Goddess. The book is inscribed to her son.

Miss Julia Townsend is the Townsends of Virginia in one person. They are today, the narrator says, just what they were long before 1776. She is gracious and unapproachable, deft at her harpsichord, accomplished at her jellies, and proud of her napery. She is a staunch Episcopalian, refined, intolerant and sentimental, but too proud to show it. Her home is Rosehill, which had more and finer magnolias than roses, though many beautiful roses grew there. From that rooted old world the tale turns to the couple of the title, whose name promises the East.
59636-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of Gutenberg works on Napoleon Bonaparte. The list names Bourrienne Memoirs of Napoleon first among its entries. Constant Private Life, Goldsmith Court of St. Cloud, and Rose Life follow. Lockhart and Walter Scott lives of Napoleon stand in the list.

Ségur Russia expedition, Henty tales, and Sloane life fill more lines. Maitland Surrender, Las Cases Memoirs, and Rapp Memoirs appear in turn. Tarbell Life, Whately Historic Doubts, and Napoleon own maxims close it. Full tables of contents for each volume follow the master list. The index serves readers who want the whole Napoleon shelf in one quick list.
60341-a-history-of-the-second-division-n:
Daniel Bidwell keeps a unit record in A History of the Second Division Naval Militia, Connecticut National Guard. The book was printed at Hartford in 1911, with copyright held by Bidwell. He gives it to all friends of the Naval Militia.

The tale is cast as a ship's log of courses. First come the years before the launching, 1890 to 1896, and the launching itself. Cruises then run year by year: the Cincinnati, the Maine, and the war year of 1898. Dewey Day, September 30, 1899, gets its own head. Later courses sail the Prairie, the Panther, the Hartford, and the Louisiana, to 1910.
61125-historical-record-of-the-nineteent:
Richard Cannon compiled the Historical Record of the Nineteenth, or the First Yorkshire North Riding, Regiment of Foot, printed by authority in London in MDCCCXLVIII. Cannon worked at the Adjutant General Office, Horse Guards. Plates aid the record. General orders from Horse Guards, January first, eighteen thirty six, stand in front. His Majesty commanded that an account of the services of every regiment be published, the orders say.

The record runs from the formation of the regiment in sixteen eighty eight through its services to eighteen forty eight. The orders require the period and circumstances of formation, with services in war and peace. Cannon follows the regiment through Flanders campaigns, colonial service, and the Peninsula age. Colonels, honours, and uniforms stand in their places. Army historians get an official regimental history, dry and exact, twin to the Sixteenth record.
61496-stanley-s-story-or-through-the-wil:
Stanley's Story was published at Philadelphia in 1890. Potter issued the narrative under copyright that year. Feather, a special correspondent, compiled it. His matter comes from Stanley's own reports and data. A front plate pairs Stanley with Emin Bey. The title page promises the whole career. Finding Livingstone, the lost explorer, leads the list. The great overland journey across the continent follows. The Congo is explored, and its free state founded. Equatorial Africa opens to commerce and Christianity in the telling. The relief of Emin Bey in the Soudan comes last. Starvation, misery, and death mark that march, the blurb owns.

A dedication thanks the faithful followers who made the work possible. Public spirited citizens who funded it share the honour. The book is a popular life of Stanley, rich with plates.
65091-preliminary-report-on-gowganda-min:
The Preliminary Report on Gowganda Mining Division, District of Nipissing, Ontario, was printed at Ottawa in 1909 for the Geological Survey Branch of the Canada Department of Mines. Collins, the survey's man on the ground, wrote it, and it carries the survey number 1075. A view at the foot of Duncan Lake fronts the report.

Collins first sets out the district: how to reach it, its hills and drainage, its plants and beasts. Then comes the rock story in order: Keewatin, Laurentian, and Huronian beds, with their conglomerates, greywacke, and arkose, and the later diabase that cuts them. The money part closes the book: silver first, then copper, iron ores, and asbestos, with a guess at what the field may yet yield.
66269-at-the-north-of-bearcamp-water-chr:
At the North of Bearcamp Water, by Frank Bolles, holds a stroller's chronicles. Houghton Mifflin issued this visitor's edition at Boston and New York. Copyrights of 1893 and 1917 stand at the front. The months run from July to December in New England. Mount Chocorua in winter fronts the book. A line from Whittier gives the invitation: to drink the wine of mountain air beside the Bearcamp Water. A thunderstorm in the forest opens the set. The heart of the mountain and a lonely lake follow.

A night alone on Chocorua and bringing home the bear mark the summer. Migration, the vintage of the leaves, and Chocorua in November turn the year. Christmas at Sabba Day Falls closes the round. The first sketch begins on July 3, 1892, in soft rain that silenced no whippoorwills.
66406-astronomy-and-general-physics-cons:
Astronomy and General Physics is a treatise by William Whewell of Cambridge. It forms the third part of the Bridgewater Treatises. Those treatises argue God's power, wisdom, and goodness from creation. The Earl of Bridgewater left eight thousand pounds for the work. The president of the Royal Society chose the writers. A thousand copies were to be printed for each. The American edition came from a Philadelphia house.

Whewell was a fellow and tutor of Trinity College. His part treats the heavens and the laws of matter. It reads nature as a proof of design. The animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms supply arguments. The hand of man is cited as one such proof. The series was a landmark of natural theology. Scientists of the day wrote theology with a straight face. This volume shows that union at its height.
67617-nick-carter-stories-no-147-july-3-:
Nick Carter Stories number one hundred forty seven is a weekly pulp issue from nineteen fifteen. Street and Smith of New York issued the five cent number that July. Its lead tale is On Death Trail, or Nick Carter Strangest Case. Chickering Carter is named as editor of the issue in the text.

The issue opens with mail terms, back number prices, and how to send money. Chapter one, An Open Question, then sets a dark and silent room. A lone ray of moonlight slips in under a broken blind slat. The light seems to shrink from going farther into the gloom. That tense hush launches the detective tale for pulp readers of the day.
68363-nat-wolfe-or-the-gold-hunters-a-ro:
M V Victor wrote Nat Wolfe, or The Gold Hunters, a romance of Pike's Peak and New York. Beadle and Adams issued the tale in eighteen seventy-four as a cheap story paper. The hero rides the open plains with rifle and knife.

Ten years of wild life have taught Nat Wolfe sharp care, even at noon. He spots a lone family in a stout wagon drawn by three pairs of lean oxen. They are bound for Pike's Peak, like hundreds of others that season. Wolfe had often helped such folk in sickness and want. Danger, rescue, and the pull of gold drive the plot.
6875-france-and-england-in-north-america:
Francis Parkman centers this fifth part of his history on Count Frontenac, the governor who stood for the French crown in the New World under Louis XIV. The preface calls him the most striking man ever to hold that post, a leader who grew with each crisis after a most unpromising start. His career runs through petty quarrels and through clashes that decided which nation would hold the continent.

Parkman follows Frontenac through war, rivalry, and rule in New France, showing how a system built on central command met a foe stronger in numbers. The volume looks back from a time when that old contest for North America had long been settled, and it weighs what one forceful governor could and could not do.
6933-france-and-england-in-north-america:
Francis Parkman devotes the second part of his history to the French Jesuits in North America in the seventeenth century. His preface calls their efforts to convert the Indians among the most striking passages of history, full of dramatic and philosophic interest. Their work bore hard on the political fate of America and on the story of its native peoples, yet had long lain in obscurity.

While infant English colonies still clung feebly to the Atlantic shore, events ominous for their future moved in the heart of the continent, unknown to them. Parkman follows the missionaries into that interior world, where faith, empire, and native nations met. The volume is both mission history and a prelude to the contest for a continent.
7069-expositions-of-holy-scripture-genes:
Alexander MacLaren expounds Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers in this volume of Holy Scripture expositions. The Genesis contents open with the vision of creation, how sin came in, and Eden lost and restored. The growth and power of sin, what crouches at the door, and with, before, after trace a devout life. The course and crown of such a life and the saint among sinners follow.

Clear shining after rain, the sign for man and remembrancer for God, and an example of faith lead to Abram going forth and coming in as a man of faith. Life in Canaan and the importance of a choice close the opening set. MacLaren preaches text by text, drawing doctrine and daily conduct from each passage with plain, earnest care.
73551-type-specimens-of-amphibians-and-r:
William Duellman and Barbara Berg listed the type stocks of frogs and snakes at Kansas. Their paper came out from the University of Kansas in 1962. It runs from page 183 to page 204 in volume fifteen. Type stocks are the first finds that bear a kind's name. Such lists aid those who sort and name wild kinds.

Museums had begun to print such lists in those years, they note. A worker can learn where a key find rests without a long hunt. Each line ties a kind to its stored first find. Snake and frog men get a brief, firm tool. The list serves labs far from Kansas.
74134-the-magazine-of-history-with-notes:
The Magazine of History with Notes and Queries, volume two, number five, came out in November nineteen hundred five. William Abbatt issued the monthly in New York at five dollars a year. One copy cost fifty cents at the stands. A monument at Cooperstown, for Clinton’s dam, fronts the issue.

Sullivan’s great march into the Indian country leads its papers. W E Griffis tells of that summer raid of seventeen hundred seventy nine. Iroquois towns fell as the forests were opened to farms. The British navy in the Revolution fills the next study. J B Calhoun recalls Robert Fulton from his own knowing. A day in the Great Dismal Swamp gives the issue its wild note. Rare first papers close it, with a Lincoln speech of eighteen hundred fifty nine. A Washington letter to Savannah stands in that choice set.
77722-ruben-and-ivy-se-n:
Ruben and Ivy Sên is a novel by Louise Jordan Miln, published in New York in nineteen twenty five. Miln had written The Soul of China, Mr Wu, and The Green Goddess. The story grew out of her earlier book about the Sên household, she notes. She moved its dates forward rather than guess at years she cannot know.

Chapter one opens with a servant who knows his mistress has refused a proposal. Lord Whitmore has asked Ruby Sên to marry him, and she has said no. The whole household and society had taken the match as settled beforehand. Only her son Ruben and two close friends doubted her answer at all. Whitmore, who never asked a woman before, means to try again despite the refusal. Jenkins, her man of ten years, knows her word once given is final.
a-ride-to-india-across-persia-and-baluch: Harry De Windt rides to India across Persia and Baluchistan in this 1891 travel volume, with illustrations drawn from the author's own sketches. The route runs from Tiflis and Baku across the Caspian to Resht, Teheran, Ispahan, and Shiraz. It continues to Bushire and through Baluchistan by Beila, Gwarjak, and Kelat to Quetta and Bombay. Desert sunrises, corpse caravans, caravanserais, and nomad tents mark a land journey of the old kind.
abraham-lincoln-and-the-union-a-chronicl:
Nathaniel W. Stephenson writes a brief chronicle of Lincoln and the Union as volume 29 of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918, with Allen Johnson as series editor. His preface cuts the task to two questions: why was there a war, and why did the Lincoln government succeed?

Chapters move from the party of political evasion through secession and war to Lincoln himself, his rule, his treasury secretary, northern life during the war, and the vote of 1864. Stephenson writes clear narrative history for general readers, with Lincoln's career as the spine. The book appeared while another war raged, and its interest in national unity has a wartime edge.
britannica-1911-n:
Letter N, which follows M in the alphabet, is treated in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on language. In its early forms the first stroke was longer than the other two. Semitic tongues shrank the other limbs over time. Greek and Latin forms tend to make all three limbs equal in length.

The first name of the sign was Nun, from which the Greek name ny comes. The sound of n shifts with where the tongue touches the roof of the mouth. It may be dental, or made at the gum ridge, the palate, or the throat. Sanskrit marks the four sounds with distinct signs. English writes the throat nasal as ng, as in ring. The sound stands to d as m stands to b, with the nose passage left open.
correspondence-conversations-of-alexis-d:
Letters and talks between Alexis de Tocqueville and Nassau William Senior, kept from 1834 to 1859, fill this second volume. M. C. M. Simpson edited the set, and Henry S. King and Company of London printed it in 1872. A journal from 1851 and 1852 opens the book.

That journal weighs the coup that made Louis Napoleon master of France. Letters from 1852 and 1853 then take up English reform bills, French moves at Cherbourg, and the health of free rule in both lands. Talk with King Leopold of the Belgians also appears. The volume lets readers hear a sharp French mind test his views on power, class, and change against an English friend.
doe-osti-3003154-measuring-3d-profilomet:
Joshua Michael Ferrigno and Raymond Joseph Kozen of Los Alamos evaluate an inspection instrument in report LA-UR-25-31255, issued November 14, 2025. The instrument is Novacam's TubeInspect, which measures the inner and outer shape of tubes in three dimensions. The tubes under study are SAVY-4000 containers, the laboratory's standard vessels for storing nuclear material. Dents and deformation in a container wall change its stresses in service.

The report tests what the profilometer can capture on these containers and how the data are processed, with MATLAB among the tools used. Prior work built a finite element model, checked against experiments, that predicts stress at deformed regions of the same containers. Paired together, fast 3D scans and the model let staff judge a stored container's condition without guesswork. The audience is the packaging and surveillance program.
doe-osti-3013012-a-general-drag-model-fo:
Zhi-Gang Feng of the University of Texas at San Antonio wrote this final scientific report for award DE-FE0031894, covering September 2020 to August 2025. The project built a general drag model for assemblies of non-spherical particles. Drag correlations for spheres are well established, but real particles in fluidized beds and fuel systems are rarely round, and models for odd shapes and crowded assemblies stayed inaccurate.

Feng's team ran high-fidelity fluid simulations with their own verified code, covering wide ranges of flow speed, particle shape, orientation, and solids fraction. Shapes studied included ellipsoids and sphero-cylinders, alone and in fixed beds. Artificial neural networks were trained on the simulation data to predict drag quickly. The model aims to cut uncertainty in designing multiphase equipment such as coal and biomass reactors.
doe-osti-3021566-public-release-of-the-m: Los Alamos National Laboratory memorandum LA-UR-26-21521, by Thomas G. Saller of the Computational Physics Group, dated February 26, 2026, is a short release notice for two nuclear data libraries, MENDF80 and MT80, prepared for the NDI data system. It documents the files' contents and format, including the U-235 data file with 618 neutron energy groups, cross sections, and heating values. A brief administrative record rather than a research report.
doe-osti-3028590-burrowing-owl-survey-re:
Cassandra L M Hendricks of Sandia National Laboratories reports the 2025 burrowing owl survey at the lab's New Mexico site in SAND2026-19322, printed February 2026. Burrowing owls nest underground in burrows, often old prairie dog holes, across the lab's desert grassland. Yearly checks of known burrows show which are occupied, which succeeded in raising young, and which have been abandoned or hit by predators.

Results are tabulated burrow by burrow, with coordinates. Sites carry names like Landfill, Penn/Ord, and Solar. One Penn/Ord burrow is classed successful with a count of eight, while several neighbors read abandoned at zero, and at least one solar-area burrow is marked predated. The pattern is the management signal: a protected species hanging on in pockets of a working laboratory landscape.
doe-osti-3374441-multi-year-electric-fie:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-015, dated June 2026, by C. Liu and T. Lavigne of Texas A&M University at Corpus Christi, sums up a multi-year study of the electric field at the North Slope of Alaska. The site gives a rare clean view of the fair-weather electric field. That field links to the global electric circuit, the planet-wide loop driven by thunderstorms far to the south.

The team compared daily swings in the field with records of electrified clouds worldwide. They also paired field strength with radar reflectivity near the minus five degree level in local clouds. The work was presented at American Geophysical Union and American Meteorological Society meetings. Arctic records like these help test how well ground readings track storm activity across the globe.
doe-osti-3374665-multi-year-electric-fie: OYESNSA got multi-year-fielded again, and this DOE report covers North Slope. The pages detail the electric findings. The climate folks get their data. The campaign was field. The data were climate. The again were multi-year. The North were slope.
doe-osti-3375177-sup-3-sup-he-separation:
A final report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0024933, by Gary Lai, Kayla Rajsky, and Colin Heye of Interlune, studies a new source for helium-3. Helium-3 is rare and costly, yet neutron detectors and cryogenics depend on it. The firm's idea is to pull it from helium drawn out of United States natural gas. Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and the Lisbon Group partnered on the work. Revision A of the report is dated June 23, 2026.

The team weighed two ways to enrich the trace helium-3. Superfluid separation uses a superleak and heat flush. Fractional distillation boils off the lighter isotope in a column. The sums show a hard truth. Making one liter of 99.8 percent pure helium-3 takes a full day. It also eats about fourteen thousand liters of helium feed. The report still maps a lab-scale prototype, its controls, and its hazards.
doe-osti-3377403-salt-to-metal-to-salt-h:
Argonne National Laboratory final CRADA report ANL/NSE-C2023-00099, by Thanh Hua and dated June 2026, studies heat flow in narrow molten salt fuel pins. The partner firm was Moltex Energy USA. In such a pin, fuel salt gives heat to a metal wall, and the wall gives it to coolant salt. Thin pins make that path hard to model. Codes must catch mixing inside the fuel salt, not just conduction.

The project tuned the SAM code against fine-scale runs. Tuned results matched fuel temperatures within two percent. Cladding and coolant values landed within one percent. One output is a three-region effective conductivity scheme for the fuel salt. It folds natural convection, mixing, and radial gradients into one property. The NekNek linked-grid method joined the fuel, wall, and coolant domains in a solve. A data bank of temperatures, heat fluxes, and transfer rates backs the model.
doe-osti-3413706-additively-manufactured:
In August 2026, Oak Ridge National Laboratory released report ORNL/TM-2026/4722, which covers additively manufactured parts for nuclear power use. Frederick A. List, Keith Carver, Chase Joslin, Caleb Massey, Thomas Butcher, and Ryan R. Dehoff wrote the study. Printed metal parts must prove they can serve in reactors.

Three parts with downward-facing rounded bases anchor the distortion study. Such shapes need supports during printing for strength and heat flow. One part had a fully machined inner surface; another was half machined. Comparing the parts shows how print choices warp final shape. Nuclear makers learn what to fix before parts face service.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-genesis-ex:
Alexander Maclaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers offers sermon-like expositions of the first four books of the Bible. Maclaren, a celebrated Baptist preacher, treats each passage as a text for devotional reflection rather than as a problem for scholars alone.

Genesis expositions include The Vision of Creation, How Sin Came In, Eden Lost and Restored, The Growth and Power of Sin, and God's Covenant with Abram. Later volumes in the series carry the method through Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers. Readers seeking Victorian evangelical preaching at its most thoughtful will find Maclaren clear, warm and richly illustrative.
france-and-england-in-north-america-part:
Francis Parkman's The Jesuits in North America in the Seventeenth Century is the second part of his France and England in North America series. Parkman calls the early French Jesuits' efforts to convert the Indians among the most striking passages of history, full of dramatic and philosophic interest.

While England's infant colonies still clung feebly to the Atlantic shore, events ominous to their future were unfolding in the heart of the continent. Parkman draws on the Jesuit Relations and other sources to follow missionaries among the Hurons and their neighbours. Readers will find here the classic account of the missions, their heroism, their politics, and their entanglement with the fate of New France.

Francis Parkman's Count Frontenac and New France Under Louis XIV is the fifth part of his France and England in North America series. Parkman presents Frontenac as France's most remarkable representative in the New World, growing with every emergency and rising equal to every crisis.

The narrative groups itself around Frontenac's governorship, his struggles with rivals and with the English colonies, and his defence of New France. Parkman writes with the vivid, dramatic power that made his histories famous, while keeping close to documents and to the ground itself. Readers of Canadian and colonial American history will find Frontenac a commanding centre for a turbulent age.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pre-Assassinati: Pre-assassination FBI wiretapping: the title of this declassified US government document, via the Internet Archive. The Norris name hints at the subject, but the catalog gives no date, no case detail. Text not publicly located. A suggestive title, thinly documented.
man-or-matter-introduction-to-a-spiritua:
Man or Matter introduces a spiritual way of understanding nature. Ernst Lehrs, a doctor of philosophy, built it on Goethe's method. Goethe trained observation and thought together, and Lehrs follows him. An early chapter tells of Lehrs's meeting with Rudolf Steiner.

Lehrs charges modern science with one-eyed, color-blind observation. It lacks, he says, a true conception of force. Descartes and Hume come in for sharp criticism. Electricity, man's competitor in modern life, gets long attention. The book asks readers to seek the soul of nature, not just its shell. It speaks to students of Goethe and of Steiner alike.
nasa-tm-19680009741-flight-vibration-dat:
Arney N. Munson, of the Test and Evaluation Division at Goddard Space Flight Center, compiled this final report in December 1967. It presents flight vibration data from the Astrobee 1500 sounding rocket, on NASA flight 16.02. Sounding rockets shake hard at launch, and payload builders need real records of how rough the ride was.

Three channels of high-frequency vibration data came from crystal accelerometers mounted on the payload support structure. Strong transient responses struck at first and second stage ignition, which is typical, and again just after first stage burnout. That later response is blamed on the anomalous release of the clam-shell heat shield. Random vibration stayed low through the transonic and maximum pressure stretches. About twenty seconds after second stage burnout, the payload began rigid body coning motions. The likely cause was the spinning fiberglass motor case unwrapping under high temperatures.
nasa-tm-19680021941-future-aspects-of-su:
Robert Jon Pawlak of NASA's Electronics Research Center in Cambridge outlines future supersonic transport navigation in this paper. Supersonic airliners need navigation, guidance, and control electronics that work as one system. Requirements studies were complete, and a five-year research plan had been drawn up when he wrote.

The goal is a hybrid avionics system that uses each navigation method where it works best. Tasks under way included a passive navigation and traffic control satellite system. Other work targeted better all-weather landing using inertial data. Strapdown sensor redundancy, fuel-optimum climb paths, and laser gyro research also feature. Pawlak presents study results, the long-range plan, and current progress.
sculpture-of-the-exposition-palaces-and-:
Juliet James wrote these notes on the statues placed around the palaces and courts of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco. She dedicates the book to A. Stirling Calder, who directed the carving work, and to the many sculptors and workmen behind it.

James praises the fair's art as sincere, skilled, and truly American in spirit. She argues that American carving came of age after the Centennial fair of 1876. Her notes guide a fair visitor statue by statue, giving lay readers a way to judge work they might else walk past without a second look.
st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-girls-:
St. Nicholas, Volume V, Number 3, for January 1878, under an 1877 copyright of Scribner and Co., opens with The Ravens and the Angels, a story of the Middle Ages. Its author is named only as the author of Chronicles of the Schönberg-Cotta Family. A front picture shows two ways of carrying the mail. The tale starts in an old city where folk called the cathedral, and thought it, the house of God.

Since the cathedral was the Father's house for all, the poor might nestle close to its gates. When Berthold the stone-carver died, his young wife Magdalis and her two small children, Gottlieb and Lenichen, were let to live in a little wooden shed by the great west gate. Inside, choir song rolled night and day. Outside rose the sighs of a sad woman and the cries of children her toil could scarce feed with bread.

St. Nicholas, Volume V, Number 12, dates to October 1878. Scribner and Co. held its copyright. Edith Hawkins opens it with The Violin Village. A front picture shows the noon encampment. Mittenwald lies on the borders of the Tyrol. Lofty mountains shut the quaint village in. Its folk make stringed instruments for a living. On fine days the gardens blossom in an odd way.

Zithers and guitars hang drying on lines like clothes. Violins by the hundreds join them there. One August morning at five, a lad leaves a gabled house. Stephan is the village goatherd. He is not more than twelve years old. Green trims his gray suit of coarse cloth. His knees and feet are bare. A whip and a small brass horn hang at his shoulder. Black cock's feathers crown his high felt hat.
the-eugenic-marriage-volume-1-of-4-a-per: W. Grant Hague's The Eugenic Marriage, volume one of four, styles itself a personal guide to the new science of better living and better babies. Hague, of Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons, saw the set printed at New York in 1916. Only the title matter and a long index for all four volumes are present here. None of Hague's counsel appears in these pages.
the-fugitive-slave-law-and-its-victims-a:
The Fugitive Slave Law and Its Victims is tract number eighteen of the American Anti-Slavery Society, printed at New York in 1856. It opens with the law's birth and a plain summary of its ten parts.

The tract notes that Congress passed the law in September 1850 and President Millard Fillmore signed it on September 18. It calls the act, in the words of a New York paper, an act for the encouragement of kidnapping. Federal officers were bound to help seize folk claimed as runaways, with no jury and no voice for the accused. Case by case, the tract then names the law's victims.
